utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. And everyone's favourite courtroom. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted, Joanna Korner, and Jasmina Bosnjakovic for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we resume, yesterday the dictates of the clock meant that we had to adjourn before we could resolve a matter that was before us. I just wish to update the parties that we are still considering the question and will give our final decision in -- in due -- we trust in the course of this day, but in -- certainly we expect by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Radulovic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I remind that you are are still under your oath, as I invite Mr. Olmsted to resume his -- to continue his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radulovic.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Where we left off yesterday was that you had returned to Banja Luka after you had visiting the Omarska and Keraterm camps. When you returned to Banja Luka, did you meet with anyone from the CSB?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. On that very same day in the -- evening hours I met Mr. Stojan Zupljanin. There was Djuro Bulic also attending, who was getting ready to go some kind of gym or something like that. I remember he was wearing track suit pants. He had sneakers on and, strangely, woolen socks. I don't know whether that -- whether that you find that unusual, but he actually did have woolen socks. And considering the circumstances I was witnessed to, I was a little bit under the weather. But I insisted - I remember that - for the Prijedor incident to be put under some sort of operational control in order to stop it. Djuro Bulic --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, Mr. Radulovic. Let me -- today let me really ask the questions and you give answers because I do have very much limited time left. Did you tell Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Bulic everything that you had observed at the Omarska and Keraterm camps that day?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told them the most important details about the harassment, mistreatment, killing of people. I talked about the ways in which people were killed. I told them that active-duty officers of the public and state security were displeased with such kind of treatment. And those who were in charge of bringing in people, these people, are the people I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's quite -- quite --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure -- I don't -- I'm not wearing my earphones, but I'm pretty sure that the translation of the answer of the witness is not recorded properly because that is not what he said. If -- if can you ask him to repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Just very briefly, Mr. Radulovic, did you tell Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Bulic at this meeting everything or at least the most important details of what you had observed at Omarska and Keraterm camps that day? You don't have to go into all the details, as we've heard what you observed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it's probably quite obvious that this was an emotional time for you, having witnessed what you had seen. How did Mr. Zupljanin react to the information you provided at that meeting that day?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that he was surprised that he didn't trust my words then. He told me something along the lines of he will look into it. And that was mostly what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall someone at the meeting saying to you, Radule, it's a war?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Stojan Zupljanin did, and that this is happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when Mr. Zupljanin told you, Radule, it's a war, after you had told him what was happening at the camp, how did you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will remember the scene until I'm alive -- until the day I die. It was the first time in my life that I cried in front of my senior officer. I started crying after Djuro Bulic started telling Mr. Zupljanin that they should hurry because they have a football game scheduled.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did they then leave and go to that football match?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did. And I started crying in front of the building of the CSB in Banja Luka. Goran Sajinovic was with me, and he behaved the same as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May I ask you, when Mr. Zupljanin made this comment to you, Radule, it's a war, you said that you began crying. But did you respond to that statement that he made; and, if so, what did you tell Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot repeat -- or I don't even want to remember the feelings. But I remember insisting that something has to be done about it, something -- some kind of reaction should come immediately. I simply believed that no game of soccer, even if it was world championships, can be more urgent than stopping this kind of criminal activities of people who were in Omarska and Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, did you think that -- that what happened in Omarska and -- or did you tell them - Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Bulic - that what happened in Omarska and Keraterm wasn't justified by this war?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. If I my quote myself, which is something I don't do gladly, I reported it in one of my reports. I even described it as genocide and fascist behaviour, the things that were happening in the camps. I think can you find this report of mine. I cannot find a more serious word to describe the events than this one, especially in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, after this meeting that you had on the day that you visited Omarska and Keraterm camps, did you speak with anyone in Belgrade about the Omarska camp? I think you mentioned yesterday a conversation you had with Marko Lazarevic --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was that around the time of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, but it's Marko "Lazovic," not "Lazarevic." I had a word with him. But before that, before I went to Keraterm and Omarska, he had called me and told me that he had some information about things happening in Omarska and Keraterm and that I should go and look into it and then report to him. And then when I returned, I first informed him first verbally or, rather, over the phone, telling him what was going on there, and then I put it into a report, a more detailed report, where I repeated all I'd said on the phone. After that, I went to Belgrade, where, together with other members of the Milos Group, I briefed, in detail, Mr. Marko Lazovic about all we've seen in the area of Omarska, Keraterm, and Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you also tell Marko Lazovic about how Mr. Zupljanin had reacted to the information that you had provided him about the camp -- or let me -- perhaps I should say lack of response?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him everything. I didn't cover up anything just as I'm not covering up anything now, neither the reaction of Stojan Zupljanin nor the one of Djuro Bulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Some days later, did you have another conversation with Mr. Zupljanin about the detention facilities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And at that meeting with Mr. Zupljanin, what did he tell you? What did he inform you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me he received information that indicate roughly that my words, my -- what I told him was, indeed, so, and that a commission is going to be formed that will go and see first-hand. At the time, I didn't know who will the members of the commission be, and later on I found out who these people were, and I found out what their reaction was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Zupljanin had received confirmation of the information you provided him. Did he receive that from Vojin Bera?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain whether he received them from Vojin Bera. However, being an operative, I looked into what information Vojin Bera might have had. And now I can say here, in front of all the people who are here in the courtroom, Vojin Bera lied to Stojan Zupljanin - and this is how we would put it in the Balkans - he lied to him about events in Omarska and Keraterm because he, among other things, claimed that what I wrote and reported wasn't true. I would like to invite Vojin Bera to tell me where are the dead people I had seen, one among whom I could even identify, one of those people down there on the grass. If he can bring that man back here to this courtroom, then I'm a liar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, who were the members of this delegation or commission that visited the detention facilities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a combined delegation. I know for a fact that Mr. Stojan Zupljanin was part of it, Mr. Predrag Radulovic, Dr. Vukic, the man who was a self-proclaimed and duke, Vozd. I think Radoslav Brdjanin was there. And a person from the area of Prnjavor; I'm not concern about that. A man who came to the fore in the political leadership, either of Republika Srpska or Krajina. I can't remember his name; I do remember that he was a teacher of German language, and he didn't even have qualifications for that. I guess he might have worked in Germany before and that's why they employed him because they didn't have qualified people to employ.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This commission that consisted of Dr. Vukic and Radoslav Brdjanin, amongst others, did you later arrive at any conclusions about why this commission was formed?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It boiled down to just me knowing that the commission was established and that they went to see what was going on in Keraterm and Omarska. I -- I used to live above the flat of Mr. Radic, Predrag Radic, and we called each other neighbour. This is something that people do in the Balkans when we want to establish and show that we're on friendly terms. Mr. Radic took me to his apartment, to a room of his, and he was, at the time, preparing his doctor's dissertation and he told me, This what I have seen is much worse than what you've told us. I don't know what he had seen. He described some of the scenes, and he was quite depressed after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You didn't mention Predrag Radic is amongst this delegation. First of all, is he the mayor of Banja Luka and also he was part of this delegation that went to the camps?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He was the mayor and he did go, according to my information, together with a group up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did he tell you anything he observed about what Dr. Vukic was doing while they were visiting the camps?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He told me that Dr. Vukic had forced some of the prisoners to raise three fingers up and to sing pro-Serbian or pro-Chetnik songs. And than didn't surprise me much because I believed he was a madman. Nothing Dr. Vukic would do wouldn't surprise me. I was an intelligence officer, and I kept gathering information about people who were of intelligence interest. And if I would present you with a true picture of Dr. Vukic, you'd be surprise that he had could find his place anywhere expect in the mad house.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take look at 65 ter 2347.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you had an opportunity to look at this article during your interviews as well as, I think, again during proofing. And it's an article from the Kozarski Vjesnik newspaper entitled: "It's Difficult for Everyone." And it's dated 17 July 1992. This article reports on a visit to Prijedor by Krajina representatives including Radoslav Brdjanin, Radoslav Vukic, Predrag Radic, and Mr. Zupljanin. Is this the delegation that you just were talking about that visited the camps?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the delegation. I don't remember this article in its entirety. I don't know whether even I've read it or whether I was told about it about some of my associates. What I remember is that Radoslav Brdjanin claimed, among other things, that that was the best example of proper behaviour or actions of the authorities in Republika Srpska or local authorities. In other words, that the way they're acting in Prijedor should be a model for the rest of Republika Srpska. I don't remember this text really. I don't see it. I do think that this text should contain a statement of Brdjanin to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I believe it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can scroll down a bit in the English version. I won't be able to identify in the B/C/S, but it says -- at the bottom there, it says: "This state of affairs in Prijedor is an example of a job well done, and it is a real shame that there are many people in Banja Luka who are still oblivious to this fact as well as to other things that might happen in Banja Luka at any moment now."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is that consistent with what you recall?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You read from the text and, of course, you were closer to what it stated there than I did. But, yes, that's the thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How do you reconcile what the delegation statement says with what you observed at the camps?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was obvious to -- it is obvious to anyone that our views were completely opposite. Nothing from this address made by Radoslav Brdjanin can be compared or be identical to the materials that I wrote. However, after this, I found out who briefed the delegation, who had briefed the delegation, who took part in briefing the delegation, and I'm not surprised at all that there is such a difference between what I told the delegation and what this other group briefed them on. Because they were briefed by Simo Drljaca and Vojin Bera, and I cannot see how the reports could have been at all similar, because I used my eyes and my reason to view things, whereas these others probably used some other means, and that's where the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness did not confirm ever having seen or read this article and then our constant objection concerning introduction of articles that have nothing to do with the testimony here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honours, this has been -- unless it's not an issue. But this has been admitted in Stakic and in Brdjanin. This witness was able to confirm that this is the delegation and also what was said by the delegation or at least by Brdjanin that is very consist with this document, and I think it corroborates what he's testifying about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what good is the article then? Under Rule 92 quater there was a decision concerning Mr. Radic, and there is also the testimony of this witness, what he stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- I was going to ask, Mr. Krgovic, whether the -- notwithstanding the minimal connection between the present witness and the article, isn't the article admissible on its own? As I understand the Rules. Yes. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1378, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 527.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, can you confirm, is this one of your team's reports?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This report is dated 22 August 1992. And it reports that a large number of Muslim citizens were killed the previous night in Koricanske Stene in Skender Vakuf area. It says it's insufficiently verified. Were you able to verify this information as well as obtain additional information about this incident?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the information which is -- you see in front of you, I wrote on the following day. That is -- that means that this was the first information about the event concerned. Because we had learned that during the previous night a massacre had been carried out against civilians at Koricanske Stene. We later verified the event, and I discussed it most with the Zivko Bojic, a member of the SJB who, among others, at the time was chief of the crime investigation service. As far as I know, he was charged with or he had charged somebody with dealing with this incident. We had a lot of information. On the same day, we learned that 208 Bosniaks had been killed at Koricanske Stene, and we also learned about the cruel way they were killed. Of all this, I informed Nedeljko Kesic, my chief of SDB, at first orally. We also wrote about it later. But this was the very first information that the service had. Before this, all this is an very short report, neither of SDB nor the SJB had any information about it. So the managers at the CSB didn't know about it, as far as can I tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: According to the information you were able to gather, who were the perpetrators of this crime?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the active and reserve police of the police station in Prijedor. It is possible that there was -- there were people among them who were not officially active-duty or reserve police officers, but most of them were. The unit was the size of a platoon. That's what it's called also, a manoeuvre platoon. They were all individually identified, so the identity of the executioners is known. It is known who killed the Bosniaks at Koricanske Stene.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you ever see anything in writing around this time-period containing the names of the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the first time, I saw it when Zivko Bojic showed it to me. If you're interested, I can add that I know that the then-minister of the interior demanded additional information about it. He wanted people to be interviewed and be brought in. He wanted those people to be held responsible for the deeds. I know that the chief of the centre -- or, rather, the police station at Prijedor, what kind of communication they had with the ministry. I -- as far as I know, Mico Stanisic was the minister of the interior at the time, and he sent out a circular, circular dispatch, demanding that all perpetrators be held responsible. I repeat that, at the time, I had much contact with Zivko Bojic, as one of the most experienced officers of public security. He was a true professional, a fair man.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he didn't misunderstand my interest in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We're going a little bit off topic here. Let me get you back on. You did mention that the minister of interior had requested information about this killing incident. Did you provide the minister with more information about the killings?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave additional information directly to Zivko Bojic. I don't know how you will understand it. But I and Zivko Bojic had good relations. I gave him all the information that I had because I knew that he would forward it to the higher level institutions or officials. The service was not supposed to investigate, go to crime scenes, carry out on-site investigations, and the like. So all the information that I had collected, I gave to Zivko Bojic, and I saw how Zivko Bojic presented that to the minister of the interior. I know about the dilemma the man was in, about the event itself. I think that he was reluctant to accept that on-site investigations be conducted in that manner, so he wanted to have his staff do it, because he didn't approve of the methods of work. There was some sort of disagreement about it. He wanted an investigative judge to go there, the crime investigator, then a forensic expert; and I believe that's where the disagreement -- how the disagreement arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, why did you believe that Zivko Bojic -- well, let me ask you this: You said that you saw that Mr. Bojic provided the information to the minister. Can you tell us how did Mr. Bojic provide that information to the minister? Did he do it over the phone, did he use -- did he write a dispatch, or did he go to Pale? How did he get that information to the minister?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he related it to the minister in writing, which was by the rules. Whether or not he had contact with the minister apart from that, such as phone conversations, I don't know. But I do know, because I saw, that much evidence was collected about the event to start the process of clarifying what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that Mr. Bojic was displeased with how the investigation, the on-site investigation, was being conducted. Can you tell us, what happened to the evidence at the scene of the crime? Was there anything that happened to it that -- during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know about it, and we wrote about it. At the level of Kotor Varos municipality, a team was set up which removed the bodies of the killed Bosniaks. The team was headed by the current chief of Skender Vakuf municipality whose last name is Vukovic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to clarify the record, I think you mentioned this that team was established at the level of Kotor Varos municipality. Was it, in fact, Skender Vakuf municipality?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did I say? Kotor Varos? I apologise. I maid a mistake because formerly Skender Vakuf -- or, rather, that part where Koricane is belonged to Kotor Varos. Actually it's the Skender Vakuf municipality. And the chief of Skender Vakuf municipality is Mr. Vukovic today, and he was the head of the team which removed the bodies of the killed Bosniaks from the area of Prijedor. I apologise. I mixed up the names. The places are close, so I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No problem. This team, were there police officers on this team to remove the bodies?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you reported all this information about the Koricanske Stene incident to Mr. Kesic. Did you also report all this information to Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I say that you did, in your written statement, say you did. Do you want to refer to that to refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm really -- this practice must be stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted. But the damage has been done. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the damage has been done. He says -- his response was: "Yes." And then there was a significant pause, and then he says: "I really don't remember." Now, I asked him if he wants to look at his statement to refresh recollection because he doesn't remember. It doesn't -- I'm not sure how this is an issue. I just want him to be more confident in his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I -- what I heard you to be saying was to actually tell the witness what he had said in his written statement. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If he looks at his statement he can confirm whether it is. I apologise -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... statement, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But can we have him look at his statement and see if he can give us a definite answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- because this is an important issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's not acceptable. You have a ruling about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But I thought we had moved on from this point because the -- however unfortunate the question and answer may have been put, it's been asked and answered. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry -- I'm sorry to overtake --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask to be very briefly heard on this matter. First of all, it's not proper for Mr. Krgovic to leap up and yell, No. He's supposed to be making an application to Your Honours not to allow this. Your Honours, this is something that is clearly a matter of some importance. And it's something that clearly we ought to sort out, and it ought to be something that is not here while the witness is listening to it. Taking his earphones, unfortunately, doesn't help off -- doesn't help because the translation is still continuing through the earphones. I really do think that the time has come, when, as you say, it's interrupting the proceedings, and we really must explain exactly why we're asking the witness to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the -- where we are at procedurally, as I understand it, is that -- and I thought that we had, at least on two occasions that this had been gone into yesterday, I thought that everyone understood. There is no objection -- that's overstating it. In the Chamber's view, it is permissible for the witness on the stand, particularly having regard to the complexity probably isn't the right word, but how long the -- the period of time that has passed since these events and the details which the evidence, particularly of this witness, involves, for a witness to be invited - I indicated yesterday that I -- and I'm used to it being the other way, but I have no difficulty with the witness being invited even by counsel who is leading him to look at his written statement and then be asked the question again. The reason why -- for the purpose of refreshing his memory. The document does not become an exhibit. The reason why I have adopted the practice of looking in the direction of the Defence is because I do not, with respect, Ms. Korner, agree that Mr. Krgovic is merely interrupting the proceedings. As I understand the position that he is -- he, at least - I'm not so sure about the Stanisic Defence - has consistently taken is that he objects to this and, therefore, for -- to preserve the consistency of his position he would probably wish to have his objection on the record. But notwithstanding that - and in my view he is entitled to have that objection registered in each case, notwithstanding the path that has been laid out in terms of the -- of how we are approaching it. What occurred in this case is that counsel for the Prosecution, as it were, leapt over the step of having the witness refresh his memory and gave the answer. And that is why I use the phrase "the damage having been done." I didn't mean it in any large sense because to my mind it's a relatively small point because had the -- had the intermediate step been taken by Mr. Olmsted, we would have been exactly where we are now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I say straightaway, then, Your Honours, we accept that. As Your Honours have pointed out, this witness made a lengthy and extremely detailed statement based on - and can I just emphasise this - based on answers that he gave over a -- in a number of interviews over a long period of time. So -- and the statement was simply a method hopefully of dealing with the Rule 92 application, Rule 92 ter application. So, Your Honours, are quite right. What my objection to Mr. Krgovic's objection is he is perfectly entitled each time to register an objection. What we say he is not entitled to do is to leap to his feet and say, No. Can he say to Your Honours, Your Honours, I want to register my objection; and that's it. But he's aptly, at the moment, directly addressing counsel and shouting, No. And that, apart from anything else, puts the witness off. Your Honours, so -- but, Your Honours, we absolutely agree. If Your Honours are -- if -- provided we follow a procedure, namely that we invite the witness to refresh his memory by looking at his statement and then asking him whether he wants to reconsider his answer. We accept that's the proper way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to state for the record that the Stanisic Defence supports the objection of the Zupljanin Defence. Only we have risen so far because we see no point in repeating the same objection as my -- as the other Defence. I completely agree with the analysis of His Honour Judge Hall. If Mr. Olmsted had proceeded the same way as yesterday, that is, asked the witness whether he wanted to refresh his memory and take a look at the statement and then ask his question again, it would have been all right. By the way it is, I think this is a matter that has been resolved. And on a different note, I believe it is improper for Ms. Korner to address Mr. Krgovic in this way because Ms. Korner has risen during this trial at least five times and said, No, or something along those lines. So I believe we should have the same rules for everybody, and we all -- we should all be responsible for what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to add something. The problem I have with the statement - and I do not rise often to object - is the way how this case is presented and how this witness is led. This is not an authentic statement of this witness given immediately after the events or concerning an earlier time-period about which he had a fresh recollection. This is literally a compilation of the OTP taken out of the context, that is, fragments taken out of the context, and they serve to delude the witness into believing that something is the way it was not. The question was about the reports that supposedly went to Mr. Zupljanin, and this is a -- the essence of my objection. The OTP is trying to introduce through the back door the assertion that this is immediate knowledge about Mr. Zupljanin's behaviour. When the witness says that he informed Mr. Zupljanin, sometimes he means that informed him directly, sometimes he means that he wrote reports. And the OTP is trying to elicit the answers that are suitable to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. -- Ms. Korner, Mr. Krgovic, I admit that in terms of my own education in the procedure of this Tribunal the meaning of contemporaneity has had to be expanded. Nevertheless, the -- the issues which you identify, to the extent that it creates a problem, I would have thought would have been -- could be dealt with by you in cross-examination. And there the matter should end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say this is the second time, first of all, none of this should have been said in front of the witness. Your Honours, if it comes to it, we may have to inform Your Honours what happened at the proofing session. However, the point is that very have available for Your Honours to see the taped records of the interviews that were conducted with this witness so that Your Honours can see that contrary to the suggestion that is constantly being made by Mr. Krgovic that we are putting words into the mouth of this witness, these are words that he himself used during the course of the interview in response to open questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. But, please, I do apologise for the form of my question. But since we're only dealing here with an answer he gave and then a qualification he gave after it, can he please try to refresh his recollection and see if his recollection is stronger. That was the point of my question, is to see whether he could give more of a definitive answer after he looked at his report. I did not mean to in any way suggest to him that he was not telling the truth or anything to that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I didn't have that impression, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, I apologise for all of this back and forth. You said that you informed Zupljanin but then -- I think you commented that you weren't quite sure. Could you take a look at your written statement at paragraph 156. And if could you just read that to yourself; and after you're done, I will just ask you the question again.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very good. Having reviewed this paragraph, does that refresh your recollection whether you had informed Mr. Zupljanin about what you had learned about the Koricanske Stene incident as well as everything else that you had learned about what was going on after it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I spoke to Mr. Stojan Zupljanin about Simo Drljaca, and it's exactly as it says in my shortened statement. Stojan Zupljanin said to me that Simo Drljaca had great influence in the Prijedor area and that he had a good standing with the politicians and the army; also, that any involvement of his, namely, the CSB of Banja Luka, along the lines that we suggested, could result in problems in Prijedor. That is, undesirable consequences. Having read this, I would now say that my statement referred to the overall situation in and around Prijedor; of course, also, with regard to Koricanske Stene. But I couldn't say in front of this Trial Chamber what exactly it was that Stojan Zupljanin answered to me with regard to Koricanske Stene specifically, or, to put it this way, after the massacre at Koricanske Stene. I think that he spoke about the overall situation regarding Simo Drljaca and Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May the document that's before us be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1379, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, before we move on to something else, which I think the Prosecution was aiming to do, I'd like to ask you if any investigation of the Koricanske Stene incident was -- was ever made? I mean, you told us that there was a team established to remove the bodies from the scene, and -- and so my question is: Was that it? Did anything happen later on to identify the perpetrators and -- and have them prosecuted or ... or was that the end of the story?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Briefly, Mr. Vukovic, who contacted the so-called sanitisation of the area, was a member of civilian authorities, as far as I know. He was chief of civil protection in Skender Vakuf municipality. Together with the assistance of the police from Skender Vakuf and some workers or those who had been mobilised into civilian defence, he removed those bodies. As for the identification of persons who committed the crime, Your Honours, each individual's was established when it comes to the workers of the public security service, as well as those who were present but were not workers of the SJB. By this I mean drivers who drove buses and trucks that had brought Bosniaks to the execution site. There were even some individuals who were members of the Army of Republika Srpska whose identity was established as well. I know this for a fact because I saw the dispatch in which the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska - at the time it was Mico Stanisic - ordered to conduct an investigation, to conduct interviewing, and to bring to responsibility those who were responsible. I also know for a fact that someone on behalf of the police station in Prijedor replied along the lines that all of those who were present at Koricanske Stene and who were members of the public security service were sent somewhere to the front line. I think to the area near Han Pijesak, Han Kolo [phoen], around that area. And that since they were now at the front line, it was impossible to get in touch with them and bring them in for questioning. This is all I know about the steps that were taken. But as far as I know - and I know this with rather great certainty - during the war, no proceedings were instituted by police against those people who had committed that -- that crime and who belonged to the public security in the sense of establishing their criminal responsibility, disciplinary responsibility, or any other sort of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, if I understand you correctly, the minister, Mico Stanisic, ordered that the perpetrators be brought to justice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly so. And I saw that in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And despite the minister's order, the only thing that happened was that the perpetrators was discharged from their police duties and sent to the front line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure that they were discharged. They were simply sent to the front line as members of police force. So no proceedings were launched against them in order to terminate their employment, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if they returned to Skender Vakuf? Or to the places that they came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They belonged to the Prijedor Police Station. I know that most of them were returned back to the service, to police force in Prijedor. And some of them, to my knowledge, work there in Prijedor to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we look at 65 ter 543.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Mr. Radulovic, if you can take a look at this. Is this the order from Mr. Stanisic that you're referring to about the Koricanske Stene killings? And it's in the middle of the page. I know the order -- this is an 11 September 1992 dispatch and it starts out with something from the chief of the CSB, but then, below that, there is something from Minister Stanisic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what I saw. And as far as I know, this is not the only document I saw pertaining to this events at the level of communication between the ministry and the CSB and Prijedor. As far as I know, there were some additional requests sent out by the minister and the ministry relating to the task of identifying and prosecuting those who had participated in the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1380.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen 65 ter 2839. But this is subject to protective measures, so if we could do it in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, is this one of your team's reports?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you could just take a read of the document. It's a very short one. Oh we can -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We hereby confirm that Bozovic and his group are being active" -- Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Actually I just meant for you to read it to yourself. I just want to ask you some questions about --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's a report dated 3 July 1992. How were you able to confirm that Radojica Bozovic or Radomir Bozovic - whichever his first name was - and his group were active in coordinated fashion linked up to the RS MUP and your centre? How were you able to confirm that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very simply. I had three conversations with Radojica Bozovic. One of them took place at the Borija mount, the second one in Teslic, and the third one in Doboj. Or, rather, the first one was in Doboj, and then at Mount Borija, and then in Teslic. I personally met Radojica Bozovic or, rather, I personally told Radojica Bozovic that was what was happening in Doboj, what was being done by local criminals, were very often attributed to him and the Red Berets members. And I informed the MUP of Serbia about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I want to keep on topic of my question. I think you mentioned this earlier in your testimony, your conversations with Mr. Bozovic. Can I confirm that it was from Mr. Bozovic yourself that you were able to establish this link between him and the RS MUP, that they were coordinating their activities?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can because I know that the Doboj CSB headed by Andrija Bjelosevic was in contact with the group of Radojica Bozovic, and Bozovic actually worked on training with the knowledge and consent of Andrija Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have on the screen 65 ter 2836.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I see it's break time. Maybe we should take a break here then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We'd resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, just for the purposes of transcript, on page 30, line 2, I said I withdraw my "intervention" not "interrogation." Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, what we have in front of us is 65 ter 2836. It's a report dated 26 June 1992. Is this one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Unless Your Honours have any questions regarding it, I will seek to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1382 Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Radulovic -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, yesterday you mentioned two Bosnian Croat police officers who were among the victims of the Banja Luka Special Police Detachment and Red Berets in Doboj in 1992. What about the former deputy chief of SNB, Mato Krzic; did anything happen to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I object to that. It's mis -- misleading. He didn't mention that there was a victim committing a crime by the Banja Luka Special Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday he did mention two names. I can look them up, if it is necessary. But he did mention two individuals; Garic and -- there was another one that I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, his name but not who committed the crime, that it was the special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, then we'll clarify that matter very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, yesterday you mentioned two Bosnian Croat police officers who were victims in 1992 of what was happening in Doboj. Can you tell us who were the perpetrators of the crimes that were against them?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were members of paramilitary formations active in the area of Doboj. I can tell you the names of these paramilitary or para-police formations, but I never did say that these two persons were victims of the actions of the workers of the special detachment from Banja Luka. These gentlemen were Mr. Karlo Grgic who was the commander of the police station in Doboj; he was killed. And Dr. Ilija Tipura, former chief of the CSB in Doboj, who died after he was mistreated. And Karlo Grgic was killed. These men weren't the only victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the two men really well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what about Mato Krzic? Did anything happen to him?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mato Krizic, yes, Krizic, he was arrested. He was under surveillance of the National Security Service employment. They started interrogating him, they mistreated him, and that was something that prompted us to ask the chief of the CSB at the time to take all measures necessary to protect our former employees of other ethnicities, all in order to ensure that they can leave the area of Banja Luka if they wished. And it was done that way, this -- the Milos Group felt obliged to assist our former employees to leave Banja Luka if they wished to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that you knew who the perpetrators of these crimes against these former police officers were. Could you provide us who they were?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell to which groups the perpetrators belonged. I cannot give you the names of actual individuals who committed all these acts. But I can tell you which groups did so. In Doboj, there were, according to my information, five to six criminal groups. Public knew about them. Some of the members of these groups have been tried for the war crimes they committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did those groups include the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not have information that members of the Red Berets were involved in eliminating either our former employees of other ethnicities. I have information about Red Berets but the Red Berets from Belgrade, if that's who you're referring to. So these Red Berets were in Doboj to provide training. But if you are talking about the Red Berets from Doboj, yes, then you're right, these were the members of Red Beret on the local level, from Doboj, who wanted to have people identify them with this group of Red Berets from Belgrade to exaggerate their importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to clarify your last answer. You mention the Red Berets. Did this Red Beret organisation include both persons from Serbia as well as locals that were from Doboj?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat: Within Doboj, there were Red Berets, people who called themselves Red Berets because they wore just these red hats, imitating the Red Berets from Belgrade. So these members of the local Red Berets committed crimes in the area of Doboj; and our group, Milos Group, had information confirming that they were also involved in eliminations of people. I mentioned two crimes, two killings, that involved two of our former employees, Karlo Grgic and Ilija Tipura.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During May 1992, were non-Serbs being arrested and brought to the CSB Doboj building?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Unfortunately, I must say that members of a unit called special unit of the CSB also took part in bringing people in. This unit was engaged there, I assume, on a basis of some kind of arrangement that they were sent there because, possibly, it was of strategic importance for them to be there instead of being in Banja Luka; I don't know about that. But we did notice members of this special detachment from Banja Luka who committed crimes together with members of these criminal groups and organisations of the local nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You said: Unfortunately there was a special unit, the CSB Banja Luka Special Police Detachment, at the CSB building, bringing non-Serbs there after their arrest. Why do you say "unfortunately"? What happened to these non-Serbs once they were at the CSB building?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, what other term should I have used instead of "unfortunately"? What I'm saying is that I am sorry that people from the CSB were committing such things, people who had worked in the same CSB as I did. That's why I said "unfortunately" because these people were responsible for horrendous crimes, primarily physical mistreatment, let alone crimes that involved stealing valuables from those who were not of Serb ethnicity. During the days of their withdrawal from Doboj, they were taking out items stolen, and it took them days to do it. There were cars and such. They also looted shops and storage facilities and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's fine. Let's get back on -- to my question. Besides members of the CSB Special Police Detachment, were any other persons associated with the police, state security or public security, bringing non-Serbs to the CSB building?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the national security and public security service from Banja Luka who were assigned to assist the Doboj service. What I know is that the employees of the National Security Service did not take part in bringing in people. They only conducted interviews. I do know that they reacted to the condition of the people being brought in. Quite -- they made quite a lot of noise about it because these people were in terrible states. An investigation was carried out for several days, especially in relation to Mr. Grgic and Mr. Tipura because these people had been employees of the security service. I personally believed that these people need to be protected, that they need to be assisted, and that was why I asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for them to be assisted. And I would like to correct something. It's not "Grgic." I said "Krizic," "Mato Krizic."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. But please, I want you to focus on my questions because I do have very much limited time now. Is what about Slobodan Karagic? Was he bringing anyone to the CSB Doboj building -- any non-Serbs to the CSB Doboj building?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Karagic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was he doing with the non-Serbs he brought to the CSB building?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He and the likes of him involved in mistreatment of these people, and usually the victims of such mistreatment would be passed on to people from national security for an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Slobodan Karagic, what position did he have within the MUP?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was in possession of an ID document of the National Security Service. I know that because my group had arrested him on one occasion, and we found among his possession this official ID, and I even remember who signed this ID. It was signed by Milan Savic. Milan Savic was, at the time, deputy chief of the security service in Doboj. In other words, deputy to Andrija Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned Milan Savic. During this May time-period, was he involved there arresting non-Serbs and bringing them to the CSB building for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was at a higher level, you see, he managed -- because prior to the war, he had been a driver, so he drove really fast and reached the position of the deputy chief of the security service. He was a big boss. It was more difficult to reach him than it was for the people who fought in the Second World War to storm a bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like to ask a few questions now concerning the CSB Banja Luka Special Police Detachment and its activities in Kotor Varos. Can you tell us for how long did the detachment operate in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think for about 20 to 30 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who was leading the detachment -- the detachment during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljuban Ecim.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while the detachment was in Kotor Varos, where were they based?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were based in the premises of a company, timber company. I can't remember the name of this company for timber processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was that also known as the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what intelligence information did you receive about any crimes committed by this detachment, in particular at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a nutshell, they committed things that were committed in other area; physical mistreatment, killing of people even, looting. If you are interested in what they did in the sawmill; namely, we received information that they were bringing in women of Bosniak and Croat ethnicity and then raped them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that you talked with Mr. Zupljanin about the behaviour of the detachment members in Kotor Varos. Did you also report these rapes to him?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to him, and I told you already that Mr. Zupljanin was concerned. I don't think he received such information only from me. From this point in time, I can say that I never covered up anything or concealed anything, and I don't see why I wouldn't have told him about rapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall whether he said anything to minimise your reports in any way?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often, during our conversations, and we didn't have that many opportunities to talk, he would always use the same comment: Well, it's wartime. Such things happen. Those were his comments. I cannot quote literally every word of his. I can't even repeat my own words. This was 20 years ago. But I do know he had been in Kotor Varos area, that he received complete information not only from me but also from the chief Savo Tepic, and I believe he also received a complete information, although a little bit belatedly, from an operative of ours, Zdravko, who was together with Pejic [as interpreted] at the time when the detachment was there. The situation in Kotor Varos was rather difficult. It was not only my qualification of the situation but also by the others who reported during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: While the detachment was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Again, an intervention in the transcript. I believe the witness gave the name of the operative that -- Zdravko Pejic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: MR. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If this can be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, you just heard what my learned friend raised. Is the name of one of the operatives Zdravko Pejic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I see mention only of chief Savo Tepic, but I also mentioned Zdravko Pejic who was an active employee of the National Security Service who was, according to establishment, chief of the wartime department of National Security Service in Kotor Varos. That was his full title.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned -- -

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, because in this -- in his previous response missing is time-frame when the report by Zdravko Pejic was submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Why don't you -- I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He mentioned time-frame, but it's not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, did you mention the time frame in which this report by Mr. Pejic was submitted? Do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember well having a conversation with Zdravko Pejic in relation to events in Kotor Varos, and, as a colleague, I asked him why hadn't he informed the service about it, referring to the National Security Service and the chief Stojan Zupljanin. I remember well; he responded, You know what they're like. And also cursed. Among other things, he also said it would be good if you do it. I don't know why he passed the hot potato to me, and I informed about information I received not only from him but from others, the relevant people, and I also know that immediately after that, he drafted a report and that only after that Stojan Zupljanin went to Kotor Varos in relation to these events. And then I also know there was some meeting held at the police station in Kotor Varos, and that's why I'm saying that it was not timely, his report to Stojan Zupljanin and the leadership of the service, because he had had such information prior to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Would this -- would these reports have been filed in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that when you had this information with Pejic he said, You know what they are like, when you asked him why hasn't he filed his reports with Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Kesic. Did you understand what he meant by "you know what they are like"?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I understood. Some members of the special detachments were feared by everyone. They were so powerful that even our chiefs were afraid of them. They will not admit that to you, but, yes, they were afraid. I was also afraid. I -- mostly because of the children, because of the threats, and their actions in relation to me and my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I want to focus on that -- my question though. You asked Mr. Pejic why he hadn't filed his reports with Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Kesic and he responded, "You know what they are like." He was -- are you saying that he was referring to the special police detachment; or is he referring to Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Kesic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He was referring to the special police detachment when he said "you know what they are like." He meant that they would be ready to avenge themselves on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now I understand, thank you. Did your intelligence team gather any information concerning what happened to the non-Serb civilian populations in two villages, Vrbanjci and Dabovici [sic], in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I understood your question even though you mispronounced the name of the second village. We wrote about it. We wrote about it, sir. About the problem and what was happening in that area, what kind of crimes were being committed. But we didn't conduct individual investigations to find out who had committed it and which individuals were involved. There was much crime, so it was difficult for a small group to be everywhere and clarify everything to the full. It wasn't our duty, nor were we able to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall whether the special police detachment was involved in the attacks on those two villages? And I'll repeat them: Vrbanjici and Dabovci. Were they involved --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Wait until I ask. There's -- we're overlapping. Were they involved in those two attacks?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. I thought that you had finished. I said, Yes. My answer is indeed affirmative. Yes, they did take part in the attack on those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what happened to the non-Serb population in those villages?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most all of them were expelled in various ways. Some of them went to Bosniak-controlled territory on their own; some went in groups, because they were let go; but some also came to harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when you say "came to harm," does that mean they were killed or beaten? What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the former. They lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you included all this information in the reports you submitted to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, everything can be found in my reports. That is why I bear no moral or other responsibility for repeating it today. I think it was much less safe to say that in 1992 because of my personal safety and the safety of my family than it is today. I stated everything I knew about these events in my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 10199.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is an Official Note dated 3 November 1992 pertaining to the situation in the Vecici area of Kotor Varos, and it contains your last name at the top of it, amongst your other members of your group. Is this one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What information did you receive from your intelligence sources regarding negotiations with the Bosniaks in Vecici for their safe passage out of Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A group of 500 to 700 armed members of the SDA safely reached Bosniak-controlled territory. We even had information that they were -- they had their personal weapons on them. We also had other information that is not contained in this report because it seemed to suggest that these people had negotiated their departure and paid large amounts of money to be let go. We didn't mention that in the report because that would point to a possible involvement of our superiors in those negotiations. So we didn't want to put a noose around our own necks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: According to your sources, who participated in the negotiations amongst your superiors?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I know that Lieutenant-Colonel or Colonel - I'm not sure of his rank at the time - Peulic must have been involved. He was a military officer. There were indications that Mr. Stojan Zupljanin was also involved, and that's why we omitted to include this information. But let me add you -- add this: We didn't keep completely silent about it, because we submitted that to the bodies of military security, the intelligence centre of the army headed by Branko Ratic of who we knew that he was very close to President Karadzic. So we didn't keep that information to ourselves after all. We passed it on, and we considered that this route was safer than the regular route that information should have been passed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: According to your intelligence information, what happened to those Bosniaks who could not pay the fee to have safe passage from Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stayed in the villages. These were mostly elderly people, women, children, and their mistreatment continued. A number of persons from that village was taken toward Siprag -- rather, Siprage; and before they reached that place, they were all killed. According to our operative intelligence, which can be seen, they numbered about 70 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned Siprage. Is that -- was that in relation to Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was done in the hamlet of Grabovica, but it is close to the village of Siprage.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. I want to move, finally, to Teslic. Can you tell us, How did you first come to hear about the Mice Group, the first time that you learned that this group was being formed?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Doboj. I had an operative presence there. And on the premises of the security services in Doboj, I met my -- I met people from my town who I all knew by name. It was the then-chief of the municipality, Nikola Perisic; then Predrag Markoscevic [phoen], a SUP employee; then Marinko Djukic, another SUP employee; then Vid Stojanovic from the TO; and there was Mr. Misic, whom I knew as a politically active man in the Teslic municipality. I didn't know why they were there, so I asked them about it. And they replied to me rather officiously that they were there to apply for assistance from Doboj because the situation in Teslic, they said, was stale. In Teslic there were many problems, so they had come to Doboj to request assistance to make people aware that there was a war on and that people had to behave as appropriate for wartime. That's what happened in Doboj. I didn't know then that the Mice Group would be sent there to help them. I only learnt about that later, when they began to harass Teslic. Savo and my brother, Nenad Radulovic, informed me of the events in Teslic --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I passed on that information --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry for interrupting. You passed that information on to the CSB?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the chief of national security, Kesic, through Vojin Bera. But I mentioned Savo. I would like to add his last name, which is Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I want to return to that in a second. But just to clarify your answer with regard to this meeting you had in Doboj or the -- this encounter you had in Doboj with Nikola Perisic. Just to clarify, was that at the CSB Doboj building?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. In the lobby on the upper floor - it's a rather spacious lobby - it is still there, only the entrance is modernised. And that's where I met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many members of the Mice Group came from CSB Doboj?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 20. That was the first group that arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who was the leader of this group from the CSB Doboj?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leader of that group was not from the CSB of Doboj. He was a member of military security. I know that he had the rank of captain. I can't remember his name now. The Mice consisted of active-duty state security officers, active-duty public security officers, reserve members of state security, and a number of members of the VRS. I don't know whether they were from the security organ or another operative unit. Among the active staff of state security I saw, Culibrk; Dobrivoje is his first name. I had worked with him earlier in the SDB of Doboj. I saw some staff of the SJB and the SDB that I knew. I'm sorry to say that among them there were some people who I had known as criminals, really bad criminals from Doboj and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were these the same individual who in May 1992 were mistreating non-Serbs either at the CSB building or other places?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Among them, there were also these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was Milan Savic's role with regard to the Mice Group?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, I didn't know. I found out only after they'd been arrested. I heard that he was actually the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where were the Mice Group members based in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At several locations: One was the Barici hamlet, about 5 kilometres from Teslic. Then there was the Kardijal Hotel, 2 kilometres from Teslic. And a number found accommodation with their lovers. I remember that well because we arrested them all at those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Before the Mice Group arrived Teslic, were there any armed conflicts going on in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But before I reply to this question, when I say "Barici," actually, it should be "Dzulic." These are close to -- these places are close to each other. They were at the school in Dzulic. And now, if I may reply to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. My question was: Before the Mice Group arrived Teslic, were there any armed conflicts going on in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no major armed conflicts. But there were three spots where Serbs did not go, nor did Croats leave those places. Stenjak, Ruzevic, as well as Slatina and Komusina. As earlier as 1991, Slatina and Komusina were the places where paramilitary units started arming themselves. They were rather well armed. And they called themselves Ustashas. At Stenjak, a group of extreme Bosniaks were rather well-armed. And at Ruzevic also, a group of Bosniaks was rather well-armed, and they even had some artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, we went from the people of Teslic coming to Doboj to ask for assistance to the arrival of the Mice Group in Teslic. My question is: Is there a link between the two? In other words, was the arrival of the Mice Group the assistance -- the answer to the question of assistance? Was the Mice Group sent in to Teslic to assist the Teslic authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you understood correctly. That is the assistance the representatives from Teslic had applied for. So the arrival of the the Mice was the assistance provided to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In Teslic, were the Serbs also arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that you learned about what the Mice Group were doing in Teslic from Savo Stanic and your brother. Do you recall approximately when you received that information and then when you reported it to Mr. Kesic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information around mid-June. I immediately informed Mr. Kesic. Then, I did not know that members of the Mice Group had killed anybody. I only knew that they had been taking people in; they had mistreated people; that they imposed a curfew from 8.00 a.m. til 10.00; that after that nobody was allowed to stay in the open; that all lights must be dimmed, which immediately made it clear to me that they didn't want witnesses, if people were not allowed to switch lights on. So the Mice were doing all sorts of things but didn't want people to witness that. And that's why they wanted all windows closed and the blinds down in midday. That was my only logical conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just for the sake of the clarity of the transcript, the witness was talking about the -- the drapes being drawn during the day-time and not -- he was not talking about the light. I mean, that was his answer. So if this can be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think that is logical without going into it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How did -- do you recall how Mr. Kesic reacted to the information that you first provided regarding the Mice Group in Teslic, in mid-June?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. He reacted rather casually. He said, What do we care? That -- that's a problem for the people in Doboj. Let's not interfere. He said something along these lines. As I was from Teslic, he may have thought that I was more interested in this area than I would have been in another.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall, did you also provide, at this time, in the middle of June, information to Mr. Zupljanin about what was going on in Teslic with the Mice Group?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After receiving information from Savo Stanic and my brother, I sent two operatives from the Milos Group to the Teslic area. I gave them the names of the persons to talk to about the events in Teslic, and I told them to inform me about what was really going on in Teslic as soon as possible. I must say that only Goran Sajinovic knew who our collaborators were. Apart from him, nobody else from the group knew who our collaborators or our operative connections were, but everybody knew our friendly connections. I gave enough information about our collaborators, and he called me in the afternoon hours and told me -- he was rather upset. He told me, Boss, the situation is much more serious than we had thought. He was, of course, joking. He never called me Boss except in serious situations. And I said, All right. Come immediately and inform me. And they did. We wrote a report.
