And soon after that, a day or two may have passed, I can't remember now, the chief of the municipality, Nikola Perisic, came to see me in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let me stop you because I want to go into that, but I want you to answer my question. And this is around the time-period of mid-June 1992. You mentioned that you informed Mr. Kesic about what the Mice Group was doing in Teslic at that time. And my question was: Did you also inform Mr. Zupljanin at that time? And we'll talk about your meeting with Perisic later.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not inform Stojan Zupljanin after receiving the first information because it was only the initial operative information. But I did inform him later, and I can tell you about his reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll tell you -- we'll go into that maybe in a second. But perhaps to refresh your recollection you could look at paragraph 106 of your statement. And just read it to yourself; do not read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'm particularly interested in the last sentence of that paragraph. Having read that, does that refresh your recollection whether you informed Mr. Zupljanin before -- well, around this time-period, mid-June, about the Mice Group in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, even without propping my memory I see what -- what this says. I remember, however, what I said. The first day, I directly informed Stojan Zupljanin about it. On the same day, he gave approval to establish a group to passivise these renegades in Teslic. It happened on the same day in the afternoon or evening hours, and that was the order and the decision of Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just hold on there for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, just for the record, I just wanted to point on line [sic] 51, 9, it's the first "day," not the first "say."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And Mr. Zupljanin -- I apologise. Mr. Radulovic, we're going to talk about your meeting with Zupljanin which was attended by Mr. Perisic in a second. I just wanted you to read that paragraph and see if that refreshed your recollection that you informed Mr. Zupljanin prior to that meeting with Perisic and Zupljanin about the Mice Group. If it didn't, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, regardless of how often you say, No, no, no, before that meeting, on that same day, I informed Stojan Zupljanin about the fact that the representatives from Teslic wanted to meet with him and explain the situation to him. And I remember very well that on that day Mr. Zupljanin attended the meeting of the Municipal Assembly. And I know that I asked him to come out of the meeting, and he did come out, and he told me verbatim to organise that meeting in the afternoon hours in the building of the security services in Banja Luka. He basically shifted to me the entire organisation of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. And, please, please, I know this is -- you want to give a lot of information about this, but my question -- I think you did answer, the answer was, No, that you don't recall providing him information prior to that date, and that's fine. My next question for you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, before we get too far off, I'm looking at the transcript, line 8, page 51, and I need clarification as to whether I correctly heard the witness say that the -- Zupljanin gave approval to stabilise a group to "pacify" the renegades in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, did you hear what Judge Hall asked? Is that a correct statement of what happened?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it's not the word pacify that I used. I received consent -- or, rather, order, not a consent or approval but an order from Stojan Zupljanin. And that was one of the first orders that he gave me, where he asked that they be arrested, "arrested," not "pacified."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, I want -- this meeting that you -- that Mr. Perisic attended, could you tell us who else attended this meeting with Mr. Zupljanin? And, please, just list their names.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't need their positions. So there was Nedeljko Kesic, there was Branko Peric, Nenad Kovacevic, Vitomir Popovic, Milan Stevilovic, Stevan Markovic, Goran Sajinovic, I was there. And I don't remember anybody else being present.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Whose idea was it to have prosecutors --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. I believe the witness says -- said, 53, line 3, Branko "Peric" not "Perisic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Branko Peric, Nikola Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we got the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Whose idea was it to have prosecutors and judges present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I suggested to Nikola Perisic that he shouldn't be alone there but that there should be the prosecutor present as well as the president of the municipal or basic court in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you said that Mr. Zupljanin gave you responsibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, if are you about to move on to something else, perhaps we should take the break at this point. It's just about that time. We alert counsel that we are in the process of making inquiries, looking at the original estimates of time that you were given, and if my math is correct, Mr. Olmsted should have exhausted his eight hours by now. But looking at what had been indicated for cross-examination by the other side, how much time is available tomorrow, it doesn't seem as if it's going to be possible to complete this witness tomorrow. And we are inquiring into the possibility of an extra session this afternoon and/or tomorrow afternoon, but I'm not in position to confirm that availability at this point. But, the -- of course, if the estimates of time given by the Defence, in light of what has happened, are now more than they need, then we needn't concern ourselves with this. But we don't need an answer now, Mr. Zecevic. We are at the break. You can think about it and let us know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in fact, I was about to raise it because of witnesses next week. We brought up, as I said to Your Honours, subject to Your Honours' ruling on Mr. Riedlmayer - he's the witness, in fact, we thought Tuesday - we had estimated that with the length of cross-examination as well as examination-in-chief, Mr. Radulovic would certainly go into Monday. No question about that. But we did bring up a further -- or were going to bring up a further witness, although Your Honours aren't sitting on Friday, just a short 92 ter witness, but if Mr. Radulovic is likely to continue into Tuesday, well then there's no need for that witness to attend. So obviously the timing is something of importance because we need to stop that final witness being brought up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before the witness is escorted back to the stand, we understand that Mr. Zecevic wished to raise something. But before he does, we could indicate that we have confirmed that it is possible to -- for us to do an extra session on Monday afternoon, which we are considering instead of today or tomorrow. Tomorrow is out. The -- but Monday afternoon instead of this afternoon. And secondly, having regard to what Ms. Korner had indicated, we think that it would probably be visible for them not to bring in this short witness that she had. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to be as brief as possible with regard to what I wished to inform the Chamber of. If you remember, some time ago -- Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may have heard what would have passed between the Court Officer and the Bench. Have you a half-hour left, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May I just beg the Trial Chamber to give me a little bit more time. And here is why: This witness has been very long-winded in his responses, and I have done my best to keep him short. And I just want to get through Teslic, and I just want to show that -- this video that you allowed us to add to our exhibit list. And I think I can do it in hour. So if I could have the rest of this session and, if necessary, a little bit of time tomorrow, that would absolutely it. But I think I might have a little bit of -- well, a bank of time from my last witness. I think I saved about an hour and a half. And maybe I could cash that in at this point. I apologise, but it's just been quite difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As I quipped the other day, this notion of the "bank," I don't know where that originated, but it's not something that we as the Bench buy into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: 45 minutes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, we're going to have to go at break-neck speed right now to try to finish by the end of this session, so please excuse me for skipping over a lot of parts that you might want to talk about. Did Mr. Zupljanin provide you with in the instructions on how to commit -- or how to conduct the operation against the Mice Group? Just tell me if he did or he didn't.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that they need to be arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that's it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me to put it in the shortest form. I was ordered to arrest them, that I must put myself at the head of this unit that conducted the arrest, and file the criminal report. That was all taken under this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how long after this meeting with Mr. Perisic and Mr. Zupljanin did you conduct the operation?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, at 0400 hours, we started with the operation, and the preparations were conducted in the course of the preceding night, starting at Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Before you conducted the operation, did you send any messages to CSB Doboj concerning the Mice Group?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was two or three days prior to the arrest. I told Dobrivoje Culibrk, a person I knew from before, that they should pull out of Teslic and unless they do so there would be a conflict. And when I said a conflict, I said with me, but I meant the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you tell him to inform anyone at the CSB Doboj within the state security service to withdraw the Mice Group?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... who?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusan Zivkovic who was, at the time, chief of the State Security Service in Doboj. I gave him a detailed explanation in relation to all the acts committed by Mice, and Dobrivoje knew about it and what the consequences will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the response that you received to your request that the Mice Group should be withdrawn from Teslic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The result was that additional 17 people joined this group, and I would characterise them as professional killers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who was leading that additional group?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Karaga. Rather, Slobodan Karagic, aka Karaga. He was somebody with a criminal record and a very terrible one, criminal record from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now we're going skip ahead because we don't have time to -- after you conducted the operation and arrested the members of the Mice Group. Can you tell us, Did you release the non-Serb detainees at the detention facilities after the operation? And just tell us if you did or didn't.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. All of them on one location. There was about 400 of them; at the other, about 600; at the third, about 140. I can't remember all the locations, but I released them all, and I apologised on behalf of the Serbian People. I told them that it wasn't the Serbs or the Serbian People who did that to them, but the Serbian scum. I used very bad words when speaking about the people who were responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were any of these non-Serbs that you released were they involved in organised armed resistance in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I didn't go into that issue. I knew majority of the people. They knew me as well. And I believed I owe that to the people who were brought in for no other reasons but for the names they bore which were different than the names of those who brought them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, on the day of the operation, did you meet Milan Savic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was arrested by members of the group I was at the head of. I know that about 50.000 German marks or other currencies were found on him, and then also some gold. All of it was seised from him. He was at first arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall if you found on him in his possession any identification cards from the CSB Doboj?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, of course. All of them. All of them who were arrested, all of them were in possession of the IDs, official IDs, issued by the National Security Service, and all of them signed by Milan Savic the man whom we arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: After the operation against the Mice Group, how long did you personally stay in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For another month.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: After during this month, did you conduct an investigation into the Mice Group? Just tell us if you did or didn't.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, detailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During your investigation, while you were there in Teslic for a month, did you receive any threats trying to make you discontinue that investigation, originating from CSB Doboj?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite a number of threats from a number of people. And the worst of them was by Mr. Stankovic who was a major at the time or may have become a lieutenant-colonel. He came personally to Teslic. He had his arm in a cast. One friend of mine helped him with that. And he came and said that he would kill myself, all of us who took part in the arrest, and our families, all of us who took part in the arrest of Mice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How about SNB Doboj chief Zivkovic? Did he issue any threats to you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime -- quite some time after the events.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992. But it -- he kept on making them for quite a long while.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During your investigation, did you learn of any mass graves where the non-Serb victims of the Mice Group were buried?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We found out about two such locations. According to our information, one contained bodies of 20 people; and the other, bodies of 48 people. We had someone who was present at the scene who explained how things came about, how the people were killed. And for the rest of the victims, where they were buried in individual graves. It was a total of 58 person killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us just generally where in Teslic these mass graves were located?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Mount Borija.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take look at what's been marked for identification, P703. And, correction, this has been -- this is not what I wanted. Let's call up 65 ter 857.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is this a letter, Mr. Radulovic, that you wrote to the CSB chief in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could see the following page and see my signature there maybe, but I do remember the content. I'd still like to see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at the second page quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I drafted this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why there's no signature, I don't know. But, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May that be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I guess it's -- has it already been admitted. Okay. That's been clarified; it's been admitted. Can we please look at 65 ter 858.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, can we just have the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit P703, to which the counsel referred to originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Here's another letter. It's dated 10 July 1992. It's from you to CSB Banja Luka to the chief of the Security Services Center personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is this - if we scroll down on the B/C/S - is this another letter you wrote?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1383, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, did Mr. Zupljanin ever respond to these letters?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. As far as I remember, no, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall, did -- did you ever have a conversation with Mr. Zupljanin about these letters?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a conversation about the situation in Teslic in general, the conditions in Teslic. We talked about insufficient information gathered about the crimes, because, at the time, I was interested in organising exhumations, post mortems, and forensic teams to do that, and I asked for assistance, believing it was necessary. So, roughly speaking, we had a discussion about what was contained in the written reports as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told, roughly, that it's not the right time for that, that there's no need for exhumations or forensic expertise. That's all I can remember. I didn't get proper assistance from anybody of those whom I had asked for this assistance, to have this issue resolved. Based on several reports of mine, one can see that I sent to -- in to an applicant [as interpreted]. I wasn't requesting because I realised that the level of cooperation following my requests wasn't something that produced results, because I even asked Belgrade to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 887. I apologise. It's 65 ter 877.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, do you recognise this article?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just very generally, is it -- is it -- what it contains in it about -- well, let me tell you -- put on record what it is. It's an article from Slobodna Bosna about the Mice Group in Teslic. It's dated 13 December 2001. Is the information contained in this article generally accurate?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one from the newspaper ever interviewed me. What is stated in the article - and I did have an opportunity to read the article - is partially true, but it is mostly just arbitrary guess-work by the author, because I never claimed that Njegos was at the head of the action or that the murder of Bosniak was ordered by the person mentioned. There are some other incorrect claims in here, but as far as the harassment and mistreatment and killings of Bosniaks, yes, I can confirm that that part is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2 of the B/C/S; page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, on page 2 of the B/C/S, the article reports: "As robbers'," referring to the Mice, "appetites grew and the amount of available loot decreased, well-off Serbs also became targets." It then describes a few instances of this and states that. "... was when the time for action came, although the police and judicial organs were quite aware what was going on in the town. Even before that, Radovan Karadzic also received detailed information." Can you verify whether that is accurate?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you I wasn't interviewed by this journalist. These are not my words, my authentic words. This is something that was taken from a different interview with me that was published in a newspaper called Nezavisne Novine. If you make a comparison between the two articles, you will see that the article in the newspaper before us is made as an arbitrary statement and generalisations of some of the information I had and then making conclusions that had nothing to do with my claims. In other words, I wouldn't say -- I would say that when journalist says that the local authorities in Teslic knew about the crimes before Stojan Zupljanin, the president of the court, the prosecutor, and the police in Teslic, they knew, even before Mices were arrested, knew about the crimes in Teslic and that part, that part is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What about the part that as their appetites grew an amount of available loot decreased, well-off Serbs were also were targeted [sic]. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's another correct claim by the journalist, although it wasn't something I had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just so you know, I'm not saying that these are something that you said. I just want to verify the accuracy of this article. If you reads further down the page, it says that: "The arrested men," meaning the Mice, "were soon released and the proceedings remained open until the present day." Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we read a little bit further down, it states that: "The members of the Doboj CSB were led by Milan Savic, the deputy of Doboj CSB chief Andrija Bjelosevic, Savic was immediately released from detention at the intervention of Bjelosevic and Stojan Zupljanin even though a bag with 50.000 marks was found on him when he was arrested." Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is partially accurate. He was released on the same day, on the day when the operation was concluded. On that day, Andrija Bjelosevic came to the police station in Teslic, Stojan Zupljanin was already there, and I was told that it would not be a good idea to have the criminal report including the name of Milan Savic as somebody involved in the incidents, and, therefore, I didn't include him in the criminal report. As far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So I want us to be very clear about this. You had a conversation with Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Bjelosevic in which they said that you should not charge Milan Savic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way. You're trying to make me say something. But there was an office in which there were a dozen people at the time. Among them, Stojan Zupljanin, Andrija Bjelosevic, Dusan Zivkovic, Dusan Culibrk, and I believe that there was Colonel Stevilovic also, people from Doboj. And there was a communication among them, people were saying things, but Andrija and me were not on good terms then. So whatever he said to me was an offence. And when I tried to convince him of anything, to tell him what had happened, he denied it. So I understood that the man wasn't well enough informed. So I can't really say now, but I do know that the CSB Doboj executives demanded that Milan Savic not be included in the operative investigation concerning his participation in that group's activities. They explained to me it wouldn't be good because he was a member of the service, like the other active-duty servicemen, so this could all be connected to the service. And I believe that I said as much in one of my interviews and gave a much more detailed explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, isn't the -- don't the answers the witness has given remove one of the grounds for admissibility of an article, namely its reliability? You have asked him about portions of it which he has agreed with and adopted, but the effect of his evidence as I understand it is that the article taken as a whole is unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As an item of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's how I interpreted his testimony, Your Honour. I think he said that there were bits of it that were not accurate but that, you know, generally it was truthful about what happened with the Mice Group. Maybe I can lay more foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And he has said that. That's as far as you need go.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I'm only giving excerpts of the article, and I'd like to have the whole article admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, that is exactly the observation that I have made. What the witness's answer to your questions have been is that the article taken as a whole is unreliable. There are portions of it which -- with which he agrees and which he accepts as accurate, and you having put those portions to him in -- in the form of specific questions, he has answered them and thus adopted it. But what he hasn't adopted in the other parts, he has said something in which the Chamber cannot rely. So why should we accept it as an item of evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, if I may be of assistance. The witness actually said: "... I did have an opportunity to read the article - is partially true, but it is mostly just arbitrary guess-work by the author." It's page 66, 18, so therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You know what, it's -- I'm sorry for interrupting. That's fine. We won't move to admit it. I have 15 minutes; I want to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned at the beginning of your testimony at the beginning of this week that criminal proceedings were initiated against you for undermining the combat spirit of the Republika Srpska and spreading brotherhood and unity by releasing non-Serbs from detention facilities. Were these criminal -- was this criminal report a reaction to your Mice Group operation?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when was that criminal report filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who filed it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The CSB of Doboj. The CSB of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a quick look at 65 ter 860.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add: Not only was a criminal report filed, but an indictment was also issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have in front of us is a report dated 13 July 1992. Is this one of your team's reports?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It requests the replenishment of the reserve police force, and it states: "It notes that their engagement in the reserve police would be good for preventative reasons since individuals from this company or their entire company had got out of control and became a paramilitary formation." Are you referring to members -- people who were working with the Mice Group?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is a group led by Second Lieutenant Jocic. Its status was undefined. And before this operation, there was a -- the possibility that these people would become our worse enemies. So we were able to persuade Second-Lieutenant Jocic to side with us and assist us in arresting the Mice. They were rather young and brave and rather well trained, and I thought that they should be placed under control so they don't become renegades.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You state here that individuals from this company had -- have gotten out of control. Can you tell us what they had been doing that got them out of control? What kind of activities they were engaged in?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this report was written to prevent them from getting out of control. We knew the composition of this units -- unit, and we knew it was headed by the former JNA officer, this man Jocic. We established contact with him later. They were drafted to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was your request granted by Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I withdrew before I could get any information about this group joining the reserve or active police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1384, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have on the screen 65 ter 2838. I'm sorry, this is subject to protective measures. So can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have nine other Milos reports that obviously I'm not going to get to. They are all part of his 92 ter package. He all authenticated them in his 92 ter statement. I was wondering whether it would be possible simply to provide the numbers of -- the 65 ter exhibit numbers for those documents to the Registrar and then those can just be admitted in bulk. We have gone over quite a few Milos reports. These are in line. And, of course, there's a written statement that can verify their authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, before I start the cross-examination, I need to know what has been admitted. Therefore, I would rather give 15 minutes of my time to Mr. Olmsted so can he can finish probably with this than wonder which of the documents have been introduced. And then I offer them again and we just use the time. I'm perfectly willing to give 15 minutes of my time to Mr. Olmsted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We have the bank again. Mr. Olmsted, I haven't forgotten you also alerted us to the video. We indicated that you had 45 minutes, which is about to expire. It's about time that we rise for the day. The -- on the resumption tomorrow, could you prove your video that you have alluded to, and the -- I would have thought that the -- given the adjournment, that, if the -- provided, of course, these -- whatever the number of the remaining documents are are on the 65 ter list ... they all are?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So the -- I don't know that you wouldn't necessarily need the 15 minutes because Mr. Zecevic could, I would have thought, put himself in the position, once you would have communicated to him what the numbers are, to cross-examine tomorrow. So the only thing left for you to do tomorrow morning would be to prove your video, and that would bring your examination-in-chief to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me just put the numbers on the record. It will just take a second. 65 ter 871, 873, 2830, 146, 2837, 549, 203, 2842, and finally, 2843. I think there are nine documents there. And, of course, if one has been admitted, then -- and that's redundant, but I think I checked and these weren't, but ... perhaps that could be verified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So the Registry would assign numbers to those five or six, whatever the number is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The numbers will be Exhibits P1386 through P1394, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I also just remind Your Honours that if Mr. Riedlmayer is not an expert, then we're not going to get him here on this weekend. So we do need a ruling tomorrow. It's still -- I reminded Your Honours two days ago that it's outstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We haven't forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We were actually working on the assumption that is travel arrangements have been fixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, they have. But, I mean, there's no point -- we can unfix them if you decide he's not an expert and therefore you don't want to hear from him. But I mean, what I mean is I want a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If he's not an expert, why wouldn't you hear him?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On what basis would he be giving evidence, Your Honours, if he wasn't an expert?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, I mean, a fact witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Hardly. I mean, he's -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: He's bringing all his photos of the mosques.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... of the mosques --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And so could we not see them without hearing him as an expert?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, Your Honours. I don't know that we've considered that a possibility. We've treated him as an expert; he's been treated as an expert in other trials. And it's -- if Your Honours decide he's not an expert -- in fact, I think we ought to -- if that's -- if Your Honours are thinking about that - I must say it never crossed my mind that you were; which shows I should never take things for granted - then we'd want to argue that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What difference would it make? I mean, we would certainly wish to hear his testimony and to see his photos. That, I think, is relevant. But the issue remains whether he has to be called and heard as an expert with all the things that follow from that qualification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He is going to be giving opinion evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is something, technically, that only an expert can do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, so long as Your Honours can say something tomorrow, one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We take the adjournment until 9.00 tomorrow morning in this chamber.
